result:
The other morning I watched a squirrel try to outwit a bird feeder that's supposedly squirrel-proof. It had a plastic dome and a slippery perch designed to send little furry bandits tumbling to the ground. This squirrel approached from below, climbing the pole upside down, which apparently the engineers hadn't considered. It reached the seeds, stuffed its cheeks with what looked like more than its head could hold, and then froze when it spotted me watching.

We had a standoff. It didn't run. I didn't move. Eventually it decided I wasn't a threat and resumed its work, occasionally glancing over as if to say, "You saw nothing. Understand? You saw nothing."

I think about that squirrel more than is probably reasonable. There's something admirable about its complete indifference to the fact that the entire apparatus was designed specifically to defeat it. It just looked at the problem, tried a different angle, and succeeded. Most of my own problem-solving involves a lot more staring at the ceiling and a lot less actual action.

The thing is, the engineers will probably read about this. The next version of the feeder will account for the underside approach. The squirrel will have to innovate again. It's an arms race measured in ounces of black oil sunflower seeds.

Meanwhile, I'm pretty sure that squirrel is out there right now, unbothered, having already forgotten our encounter entirely. It's a good reminder that the world keeps spinning and the clever little creatures among us find their way through, one acrobatic workaround at a time. Sometimes I wish I had even a fraction of that energy before my second cup of coffee.
